prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part B048 configuration, crediting Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye, and my position is firmer than in round 1 because the exchange tested the objections that mattered and none of them survived as a reason to prefer something else. The scientific core is not disputed in any of the eight statements: magic-wavelength trapping cancels the lattice light shift while a large ensemble of neutral atoms sits in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which is what turns a good clock into one with both accuracy and stability at the 1e-18 level. What persuades me as an experimentalist is the independent reproduction. Several laboratories and several species reach comparable uncertainties and their comparisons agree, which is the test I apply to any claimed result. The chair's questions asked for the chronology to be checked against primary papers, and I cannot do that from my own expertise; I take Katori's 2003 magic-wavelength proposal and early strontium demonstrations as the concept and first realisation, and Ye's group as the route to record accuracy and the many-body understanding of the systematics, as the atomic-physics members describe them, and I would ask the committee to confirm this against the 2003 to 2005 papers and the later accuracy records before the vote is final. Credit to two names is the cleanest on the list, and no other shortlisted entry gives a defensible set of at most three names with this little dispute.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains distinctness from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and I want the citation to answer it by naming the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength ensemble idea rather than precision timekeeping in general. A second objection is that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg and the Yb and Hg groups made real contributions that two names cannot capture. That is a cost of the three-person limit, not a reason to prefer an entry with a worse credit problem, and I would revisit it only if a colleague shows from primary papers that one of them is a decisive third contributor. A third objection is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I do not think the science improves by waiting, but I accept that a member could reasonably weigh timing differently. Finally, I have a real weakness: I am not an atomic physicist, and my own first choice from the opening, IceCube, is a field I know better and may still be underrating.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first and flags distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the open question.
responses.response: I think the distinctness question should be answered in the citation itself. The comb gave a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems; the lattice clock needs a different idea, interrogating many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the trap does not shift the transition. I would ask Lindroth, as the atomic-physics member closest to this, to say plainly whether she regards the 2003 proposal and the first strontium demonstrations as firm priority, because that decides how I weigh Katori against Ye and whether any third name has a claim. I will accept her answer over my own recollection.

responses.point: Olsson says the clock is a distinct invention but asks for a check of the 2003 to 2005 record and still regards Higgs as the purest original experiment on the list.
responses.response: I share the instinct that Higgs is the purest original experiment, and as a detector person I respect what ATLAS and CMS did. But I reach the same obstacle she describes: Danielsson and Olsson already propose different triples from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and nobody has offered a rule I could defend for dropping one of four. A prize that cannot explain who is excluded from two collaborations of thousands is worse than a modest novelty question. I support her request to check the chronology against primary papers and would take her view of the Tokyo disclosure as disclosure only.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from the EHT to the clock because the Falcke, Doeleman and Zensus triple rests on work by many people outside it, and he presses that the IceCube diffuse-flux origin is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree and I have moved the same way for the same reason. On IceCube I accept his point that the diffuse flux is secure but its origin is not, and that source identifications such as NGC 1068 are still at modest significance, so I no longer treat B033 as ready this year. On the EHT I accept that the shadow-size gravity test is model dependent and that imaging and station leaders are left out of the triple, so I keep B052 and B033 only as alternatives, not as a second part.

responses.point: Mehlig wants the citation worded narrowly around the lattice clock and would be more concerned if either Katori or Ye were dropped than about how the credit is split between them.
responses.response: I take both points. My revised citation names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength ensemble so that it cannot be read as a general precision-timekeeping prize, and I do not claim to adjudicate the proportions between Katori and Ye. I read his remark as a reason to keep both names and to treat the split as not a committee issue. I also agree with him that the pending redefinition of the second should not by itself change the timing.

responses.point: Johansson accepts the case rests on the diffuse IceCube flux but says the origin is unresolved and the credit underplays AMANDA, Baikal and other founders, and he says the redefinition should be neither a reason to wait nor to act.
responses.response: I accept his maturity point on B033 and the credit point on AMANDA and Baikal, which I cannot fully resolve from what we have. On the redefinition I agree it should not drive our timing in either direction: it follows from the science, and our decision is about the physics. I also take the chair's question on a second part seriously, and my answer is that no shortlisted entry gives a credit set within the one remaining name that the members who raised concerns would accept, so I do not propose a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, on primary papers, confirms Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock, and the later record accuracy and many-body contribution of Ye's group, which I take from colleagues and not from my own expertise.
Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the proposed citation wording makes that clear.

Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or another lattice-clock contributor has a documented claim strong enough to join or displace one of the two names; I would expect the three-person limit to be the reason for any exclusion.
Whether a second prize part is needed. I see none with a defensible credit set within the remaining capacity, so I treat it as unlikely.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Katori, Ye or their laboratories. For the record, my own field is astroparticle physics and detector development (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur), so IceCube and the EHT lie close to my work, though I have no personal or institutional tie to Halzen, Karle or the EHT leaders. As chair I will record the flags disclosed in round 1 (Johansson on B001, Eriksson as 2025 chair, Olsson's Tokyo fellowship, Kroll's Boulder history) and note that none touches the B048-only configuration.
